questions.scenario: A Data Engineer reviews SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY for a reporting warehouse. A web application runs SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = <value> thousands of times a day, with a different customer ID each time. Each execution is fast. The Engineer needs the total time this one statement shape used over the last 30 days.
questions.stem: Which grouping should the Engineer use?

options.text: GROUP BY query_id
GROUP BY query_parameterized_hash
GROUP BY query_hash
GROUP BY query_tag

explanation.correct: query_parameterized_hash is computed after literals used with =, !=, >= or <= are replaced by parameters. All executions that differ only in the customer ID share one value, so grouping by it gives the total for the statement shape.

distractors.A: query_id is unique to every single execution, so grouping by it never combines runs.
distractors.C: query_hash is computed from the normalized text including literals. Each customer ID produces a different value, so the executions fall into thousands of separate groups.
distractors.D: query_tag only reflects what the application set in the QUERY_TAG session parameter. It does not identify a statement shape and may be empty.

questions.scenario: A Data Engineer investigates a query that filters a 2 TB EVENTS table on EVENT_DATE and runs for several minutes. In the Query Profile, the TableScan on EVENTS shows Partitions scanned 9,850 and Partitions total 10,000. A Filter operator directly above the scan removes about 99% of the rows. The table is loaded from many sources in no particular date order.
questions.stem: What should the Engineer do to reduce the scan time?

options.text: Resize the warehouse from Medium to 2X-Large to scan more partitions in parallel
Rewrite the query to use UNION ALL instead of UNION
Raise the maximum cluster count on a multi-cluster warehouse
Define a clustering key on EVENT_DATE

explanation.correct: Almost every micro-partition was read and then a Filter discarded nearly all rows, which means the storage order is not correlated with the filter column. A clustering key on EVENT_DATE organizes the data so that pruning can skip most partitions.

distractors.A: A larger warehouse reads the same 9,850 partitions faster at a higher cost. It does not reduce how many partitions are scanned.
distractors.B: UNION versus UNION ALL affects duplicate elimination in queries that combine result sets. The profile shows a poor-pruning problem on a single table scan.
distractors.C: More clusters help with concurrent queries that are queued. This is a single slow query and the clusters do not change what is scanned.

questions.scenario: A nightly aggregation runs alone on an X-Small warehouse. Its Query Profile shows a large value for Bytes spilled to remote storage, and most of the time is in Remote Disk IO. No queries are queued.

options.text: Run the job on a larger warehouse, or in smaller batches
Convert the warehouse to multi-cluster with a higher maximum cluster count
Change the scaling policy from Economy to Standard on the warehouse
Raise STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS so the job can run longer

explanation.correct: Spilling happens when intermediate results exceed warehouse memory and local disk. A larger warehouse provides more memory and local disk, and smaller batches reduce the size of the intermediate results. Both remove the spill.

distractors.B: Additional clusters add capacity for concurrent queries. A single job still runs on one cluster with the same memory.
distractors.C: The scaling policy controls when a multi-cluster warehouse starts or shuts down clusters. It does not add memory to the query, and nothing is queued here.
distractors.D: The timeout only decides when a long statement is cancelled. It does not reduce the spilling that makes the job slow.

questions.scenario: A report query returns far more rows than expected and runs for 40 minutes. The Data Engineer sets the session variable lid to the report's query ID and runs: SELECT operator_id, operator_attributes, operator_statistics:output_rows / operator_statistics:input_rows AS row_multiple FROM TABLE(GET_QUERY_OPERATOR_STATS($lid)) WHERE operator_type = 'Join' ORDER BY step_id, operator_id; One join returns a row_multiple of about 116.
questions.stem: What does this indicate, and what should the Engineer do?

options.text: The join prunes efficiently, so no tuning of the query is needed
The query uses UNION where UNION ALL is enough, so it must be rewritten
The join is exploding, so its join condition should be reviewed
The join spills to remote storage, so a larger warehouse is required

explanation.correct: A Join that outputs about 116 rows for every input row is an exploding join. A typical cause is a missing or too loose join condition, such as an unintended Cartesian product, so the Engineer should review the condition.

distractors.A: Pruning is measured by partitions scanned versus partitions total on a TableScan. The ratio of output to input rows on a Join says nothing about pruning.
distractors.B: UNION without ALL appears as a UnionAll operator with an extra Aggregate, not as a Join with a high row multiple.
distractors.D: Spilling is reported in the spilling statistics as bytes spilled to local or remote storage. It is not indicated by the row multiple.

questions.scenario: An Enterprise edition account has one Medium warehouse used by 60 analysts. Every morning at 9:00 the dashboards slow down. QUERY_HISTORY shows high queued_overload_time for those queries. Their execution_time is normal and nothing is spilled.
questions.stem: How can this be resolved MOST cost effectively?

options.text: Resize the warehouse to 4X-Large and keep a single cluster
Convert it to multi-cluster with a higher maximum cluster count
Enable the query acceleration service on the warehouse
Add a clustering key to each table the dashboards read

explanation.correct: High queued_overload_time with normal execution time means the warehouse is overloaded by concurrency. A multi-cluster warehouse (Enterprise edition or higher) starts extra clusters when queries queue and shuts them down afterwards, so the cost is incurred only at peak times.

distractors.A: A larger size makes each query faster but pays for a 4X-Large around the clock, and execution times here are already normal. It is not the cost-effective way to add concurrency.
distractors.C: Query acceleration offloads parts of large scans for individual queries. It does not add capacity for many concurrent short queries.
distractors.D: Clustering reduces the data scanned by queries. The queries here run quickly once started, so the delay comes from queuing.

questions.scenario: A Data Engineer's role has MONITOR on the warehouse ETL_WH. The role is not ACCOUNTADMIN and has no access to the shared SNOWFLAKE database. A user reports that something ran slowly on ETL_WH yesterday, and the Engineer wants to list the statements that other users ran on that warehouse during the last 3 days.
questions.stem: Which TWO approaches can the Engineer use?

options.text: Query the ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY view filtered on ETL_WH
Open Query History in Snowsight and filter on the warehouse ETL_WH
Query the ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_LOAD_HISTORY view for ETL_WH
Open the Grouped Queries view in Snowsight and filter on ETL_WH
Call INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY_BY_WAREHOUSE for ETL_WH

explanation.correct: MONITOR or OPERATE on a warehouse lets a role see other users' queries that ran on it, both in Snowsight Query History and through the INFORMATION_SCHEMA QUERY_HISTORY table functions. Neither needs access to the SNOWFLAKE database, and 3 days is inside the 7-day window of the table function.

distractors.A: ACCOUNT_USAGE views live in the shared SNOWFLAKE database. A role without access to that database cannot query them, and by default only ACCOUNTADMIN has it.
distractors.C: WAREHOUSE_LOAD_HISTORY is also an ACCOUNT_USAGE view, and it reports average running and queued load per interval, not individual statements.
distractors.D: Grouped Queries needs ACCOUNTADMIN, IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on the SNOWFLAKE database, or the GOVERNANCE_VIEWER database role. MONITOR on a warehouse does not grant that view.

questions.scenario: A query runs SELECT * FROM products WHERE product_name LIKE '%trail%' against a 5 TB PRODUCTS table. Query Insights reports a LIKE filter with a leading wildcard, and nearly all micro-partitions are scanned. The business confirms that matching only names that start with "trail" would be acceptable.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions reduce the amount of data scanned?

options.text: Raise the maximum cluster count on the warehouse for the job
Change LIKE to ILIKE so the filter ignores letter case
Enable search optimization on the table for PRODUCT_NAME
Change the pattern to 'trail%' so it has no leading wildcard
Run the query on a Snowpark-optimized warehouse instead

explanation.correct: A pattern that does not start with a wildcard can use the column's min and max metadata to skip micro-partitions. If a leading wildcard must stay, search optimization supports LIKE and ILIKE and speeds up the lookup. Both change how much data is read.

distractors.A: Extra clusters add capacity for concurrent queries. One query still reads the same micro-partitions.
distractors.B: ILIKE only makes the comparison case-insensitive. The leading wildcard remains, so the same partitions are scanned.
distractors.E: A Snowpark-optimized warehouse has more memory per node, which helps memory-bound workloads. It does not change which micro-partitions are read.

questions.scenario: A Data Engineer reviews Query Insights for several statements.
questions.stem: Which THREE of the following will NOT produce any Query Insights?

options.text: A single-step join of two permanent tables with no join condition
A query whose result is served from the persisted query result
A single-step UNION of two permanent tables with disjoint rows
A SELECT against a hybrid table that filters on its primary key
An EXPLAIN statement for a query on two permanent tables

explanation.correct: Query Insights are not produced for queries that reuse a persisted result, for hybrid table queries, or for EXPLAIN statements. They are also skipped for multi-step plans, secure objects, Native App queries and interactive tables.

distractors.A: A join with no join condition is a documented insight under the JOIN topic. A single step on permanent tables is eligible.
distractors.C: UNION on inputs that never overlap is flagged as an unnecessary UNION DISTINCT, with the advice to use UNION ALL.

questions.scenario: A Data Engineer must find out whether a query that ran 30 days ago spilled to storage and how long it waited in the warehouse queue.

options.text: ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY still holds its spill and queue-time columns
The Snowsight Query Profile still shows the spilling statistics for it
The role needs access to the shared SNOWFLAKE database, held by ACCOUNTADMIN
GET_QUERY_OPERATOR_STATS can still return the operator statistics for it
The INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY table function can still return its row

explanation.correct: The ACCOUNT_USAGE view keeps 365 days of history with bytes_spilled_to_* and queued_overload_time columns, so a 30-day-old query is covered. Reading it requires access to the shared SNOWFLAKE database, which by default only ACCOUNTADMIN has.

distractors.B: Query details and the Query Profile are available only for the last 14 days.
distractors.D: GET_QUERY_OPERATOR_STATS works only for completed queries from the past 14 days.
distractors.E: The INFORMATION_SCHEMA table functions cover only the last 7 days.

questions.scenario:
A Data Engineer runs the query below on a busy account. It returns no rows, although the Engineer knows several queries that ran longer than 10 minutes in the last 2 days.

SELECT query_id, total_elapsed_time
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY())
WHERE total_elapsed_time > 600000
ORDER BY total_elapsed_time DESC;
questions.stem: Why does the query return no rows, and what should the Engineer change?

options.text: The function returns only the last 24 hours, so ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY is needed
total_elapsed_time cannot be filtered in a table function, so a view is needed
RESULT_LIMIT (default 100) is applied before the WHERE clause, so raise RESULT_LIMIT
The function ignores ORDER BY, so the filter must move into a HAVING clause

explanation.correct: The table function first returns at most RESULT_LIMIT rows (default 100, maximum 10000) and only then applies the WHERE clause. On a busy account the 100 most recent queries contain none above 10 minutes. A larger RESULT_LIMIT, together with an END_TIME_RANGE_START, covers the period of interest.

distractors.A: The INFORMATION_SCHEMA table function covers the last 7 days, not 24 hours, so the 2-day period is in range.
distractors.B: Table function output can be filtered on any returned column, including total_elapsed_time.
distractors.D: ORDER BY and WHERE work normally on the output. HAVING applies to aggregates and would not change how many rows the function returns.

questions.scenario: A nightly MERGE into a 400 GB table takes 25 minutes on a Medium warehouse that only this job uses. In QUERY_HISTORY, transaction_blocked_time is about 1,350,000 ms, queued_overload_time is 0, compilation_time is small, and nothing spilled.

options.text: Find the concurrent statement that changes the same table and stagger the schedules
Resize the warehouse to Large so the MERGE has more compute and finishes sooner
Convert the warehouse to multi-cluster so that the MERGE gets its own cluster
Enable the query acceleration service on the warehouse to speed up the MERGE

explanation.correct: About 22 of the 25 minutes were spent blocked on a transaction, which means another statement held a lock on the table. The wait is removed by finding and rescheduling the competing DML, not by adding compute.

distractors.B: A larger warehouse speeds up execution, but the query is waiting on a lock and not using compute during that time.
distractors.C: Extra clusters help when queries queue on an overloaded warehouse. The queue time here is 0 and the wait is on a table lock.
distractors.D: Query acceleration offloads eligible scan work. It does not release a lock held by another transaction.

questions.scenario: An Enterprise edition account has a multi-cluster warehouse with MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT 1, MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT 4 and the Economy scaling policy. Each morning, queries queue for several minutes while only one cluster runs.
questions.stem: What is the smallest change that reduces the queuing?

options.text: Raise MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT from 4 to 8 so that more clusters can start
Resize the warehouse to the next larger size so each query runs faster
Lower AUTO_SUSPEND to 60 seconds so the warehouse restarts more often
Change the scaling policy from Economy to Standard on the warehouse

explanation.correct: The Economy policy starts an additional cluster only when there is enough load to keep it busy for a while, so queries can stay queued. The Standard policy starts clusters to prevent queuing. Only one of four clusters runs, so the maximum is not the limit.

distractors.A: The warehouse is using one of its four allowed clusters, so a higher maximum changes nothing.
distractors.B: A larger size speeds up individual queries, but it changes neither the queue nor how clusters start, and it raises the cost of every cluster.
distractors.C: AUTO_SUSPEND controls idle time before suspension. It has no effect on queuing while the warehouse is busy.

questions.scenario: A dashboard runs the same aggregate queries against the same tables every 10 minutes. The warehouse has AUTO_SUSPEND = 60, and percentage_scanned_from_cache is close to 0 for every run, so each run reads from remote storage. Result reuse is not possible because the data changes between runs.
questions.stem: What change MOST cost effectively reduces the scan time?

options.text: Resize the warehouse from Small to 2X-Large so each scan runs faster
Increase AUTO_SUSPEND so the warehouse keeps its cache between runs
Set USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE for the session that runs the dashboard
Enable the query acceleration service on the dashboard's warehouse

explanation.correct: The warehouse cache holds data read from storage only while the warehouse is running. With a 60-second suspend, the cache is lost between runs, so a longer AUTO_SUSPEND lets later runs read from cache at the cost of some idle time.

distractors.A: A larger warehouse still starts every run with an empty cache and costs much more per second.
distractors.C: USE_CACHED_RESULT controls reuse of persisted results. Turning it off removes a cache and cannot help.
distractors.D: Query acceleration is billed for the serverless compute it uses and targets large scans of single queries. It does not fix a cache lost to suspension.

questions.scenario: The Query Profile of a monthly report shows an Aggregate node above a UnionAll node. The Aggregate node uses about 40% of the query time. The query combines three tables with UNION.

options.text: Query acceleration removes the Aggregate step from the query plan
The optimizer adds an Aggregate for every UNION, so it cannot be avoided
The Aggregate removes duplicate rows, which is what UNION requires
Replacing UNION with UNION ALL always returns exactly the same rows
If the tables hold no duplicates, UNION ALL returns the same rows without it

explanation.correct: UNION removes duplicates, which Snowflake performs as an Aggregate above a UnionAll. When the inputs cannot contain duplicates, UNION ALL returns the same rows and skips that step.

distractors.A: Query acceleration offloads parts of eligible scans and does not change the plan to remove the duplicate-elimination step.
distractors.B: The Aggregate exists only because UNION is used. UNION ALL does not need it.
distractors.D: UNION ALL keeps duplicates. It returns the same rows only when the inputs contain none.
